chapters.title: The Essentialist
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to stop trying to do everything and to pursue less but better: find the few things that truly matter and put your full effort there. He sets the Essentialist, a person who deliberately picks the vital few, against the Nonessentialist, a person who says yes to almost everything and is spread thin. His method runs in order: explore, which means sorting the vital few from the trivial many; eliminate, which means cutting the rest; and execute, which means making the vital few as easy as possible to get done. He warns of what he calls the clarity paradox: clarity brings success, success brings more options and requests, and those scatter effort. His core rule is that if you do not set your priorities, someone else will set them for you. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: After his daughter was born, he left his wife and the baby in the hospital to attend a client meeting because he felt he was expected to, and he came away convinced he had made the wrong trade, giving up what mattered most for what someone else wanted.

chapters.title: Choose: The Invincible Power of Choice
chapters.keys: McKeown says to remember that you always have the power to choose how you spend your time and energy, and to use it on purpose. He treats choice as an action you take, not a thing you have, and says people forget this and come to feel they have no say: learned helplessness, the state of giving up because you believe your choices make no difference. His reason is that when you surrender your right to choose, others will choose for you. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: He describes experiments by Martin Seligman and Steve Maier in which dogs that had no way to stop shocks later stopped trying to escape even when escape was easy.

chapters.title: Discern: The Unimportance of Practically Everything
chapters.keys: McKeown says almost everything is noise and only a very few things are exceptionally valuable, so before you commit, take time to sort out those few. He uses the idea of the vital few and the trivial many, the Pareto principle that a small share of efforts produces most of the results. His reason is that efforts are not equal: some yield vastly more than others, so treating everything as equally important wastes you on the trivial. The Essentialist therefore holds back from committing and explores first, while the Nonessentialist treats every opportunity as worth taking. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Warren Buffett, he says, made most of his fortune from a small number of investments and chose to pass on nearly everything else; he also tells how Joseph Juran applied the vital few idea to quality control and Japanese manufacturers adopted it.

chapters.title: Trade-Off: Which Problem Do I Want?
chapters.keys: McKeown says to accept that you cannot have it all: every yes is a no to something else, so face the trade-off, meaning the choice of one thing at the cost of another, and make it on purpose. The Nonessentialist asks how to fit everything in; the Essentialist asks which problem he wants, and what he can go big on. His reason is that if you refuse to choose between options, the choice gets made for you by others or by circumstance. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Southwest Airlines chose to give up things like meals and assigned seats to run a low-cost, point-to-point airline, while Continental Lite tried to copy the low-cost model and keep its full-service offer at the same time, and lost a great deal of money.

chapters.title: Escape: The Perks of Being Unavailable
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to build time and space into your schedule to escape, think and reflect, because you cannot find the vital few if you are always busy. He calls for space to design, space to concentrate, and space to read, and says to make this time deliberately rather than waiting for it to appear. His reason is that without room to stand back and think, you cannot sort the vital few from the trivial many. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Bill Gates regularly took a Think Week away from daily work to read and reflect, and LinkedIn chief executive Jeff Weiner blocked out stretches of empty time in his calendar each day to think.

chapters.title: Look: See What Really Matters
chapters.keys: McKeown says to act as a journalist of your own life: look past the facts and find the lead, the one point that really matters. His steps are to keep a journal, to get out into the field and see the problem firsthand, to watch for what is unusual or out of place, and to clarify the question you are really trying to answer. His reason is that what matters most is often hidden among the details, and you must actively look for it. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Nora Ephron's high school journalism teacher gave the class the facts of an announcement that the whole faculty would attend a conference next Thursday, with a list of well-known speakers, and had them write the lead; when they led with the facts, he told them the real lead was that there would be no school next Thursday. Ephron said the lesson, that journalism means finding the point, stayed with her.

chapters.title: Play: Embrace the Wisdom of Your Inner Child
chapters.keys: McKeown says to make room for play, meaning activity done for its own sake and enjoyment, in your life and at work. He treats play as essential, not as a waste of time, and draws on Stuart Brown, founder of the National Institute for Play. His reason is that play broadens the range of options you can see, reduces stress, and helps the parts of the brain we use to plan, prioritize and decide. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Stuart Brown's research on young men who had committed murder found that a lack of play in childhood was a common thread among them.

chapters.title: Sleep: Protect the Asset
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to protect the asset, which is yourself, by treating sleep as a priority and not something to sacrifice. He says the Nonessentialist sees sleep as a luxury or a sign of weakness, while the Essentialist sees it as necessary for doing the vital few well. His reason is that sleep sharpens our ability to think, make connections and prioritize, so cutting it degrades our performance. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: K. Anders Ericsson's study of violinists found that the best performers practiced the most and also slept more than the others, including naps during the day.

chapters.title: Select: The Power of Extreme Criteria
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to use extreme criteria, meaning a very high bar for deciding what gets in, instead of broad criteria that let almost anything through. His tool is the 90 percent rule: rate an option on its most important criterion from 0 to 100, and if it scores below 90, treat it as a 0 and reject it. He also cites the rule that if an opportunity is not a clear and enthusiastic yes, it is a no. His reason is that broad criteria leave you saying yes to too much and stuck with the merely good instead of the best. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Derek Sivers uses the rule that if he does not feel a strong, unambiguous yes about something, he says no to it.

chapters.title: Clarify: One Decision That Makes a Thousand
chapters.keys: McKeown says to set an essential intent, one clear decision about what you or your team is aiming at that settles a thousand later decisions. An essential intent, as he defines it, is both inspiring and concrete, both meaningful and measurable, unlike vague mission statements or narrow quarterly goals. His reason is that when people lack clarity of purpose, they waste energy on politics and on their own agendas instead of on the work that matters. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Martha Lane Fox, in her role promoting digital inclusion in the UK, set a single concrete intent to get people across the country online, which guided her later choices.

chapters.title: Dare: The Power of a Graceful "No"
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to have the courage to say no, firmly and gracefully, to whatever is not essential. His tools include separating the decision from the relationship, saying no without using the word no, focusing on the trade-off, accepting the awkward pause, giving a soft no or a no but, saying let me check my calendar and get back to you, asking a boss which other task to deprioritize, and offering what you are willing to do instead. His reason is that you trade some short-term popularity for long-term respect. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Cynthia Covey recalls that her father, Stephen R. Covey, took her to San Francisco, and when an old college friend invited him to dinner he declined so he could keep his time with her.

chapters.title: Uncommit: Win Big by Cutting Your Losses
chapters.keys: McKeown says to cut your losses and walk away from commitments that no longer serve you, instead of pouring more into them because of what you have already spent. He names sunk-cost bias, the tendency to keep investing in something because of what has already gone into it, and the endowment effect, valuing something more just because you own it. His tools include pretending you do not yet own it and asking how much you would give to get it now, admitting mistakes, getting over the fear of wasting, stopping casual commitments, and the reverse pilot, which means quietly stopping something to see whether anyone notices. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: The British and French governments kept funding the Concorde supersonic jet for years even though it was clear it would never make back what was spent on it.

chapters.title: Edit: The Invisible Art
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to edit your life the way a good editor edits a film or a manuscript: cut what does not belong so the essential stands out. His editing steps are to cut out options, to condense so you do more with less, to correct so you stay on course, and to edit less, knowing when not to interfere. His reason is that removing the trivial is what makes the important more visible and more powerful, even though good editing goes unseen. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Jack Dorsey said he sees his role as chief executive as being the company's chief editor: of the many things the company could do, his job is to choose the one or two that really matter.

chapters.title: Limit: The Freedom of Setting Boundaries
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to set clear boundaries in advance, so you are not drawn into other people's priorities one small exception at a time. His tools include defining your deal-breakers, deciding ahead of time where you will not go, and recognizing when someone else's problem is not yours to solve. His reason is that boundaries free you, because you no longer have to decide each request on the spot, and that holding a rule all of the time is easier than holding it most of the time. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Clayton Christensen, as a student at Oxford, had a firm rule not to play basketball on Sundays and kept to it even when it meant missing the championship game, and he later said it was easier to keep a commitment always than almost always.

chapters.title: Buffer: The Unfair Advantage
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to build a buffer, meaning extra room in time and resources, to absorb the problems you know will come. His steps are to add 50 percent to your estimate of how long a task will take and to plan for different scenarios. His reason is that people routinely underestimate how long things take, even tasks they have done before, which the psychologist Daniel Kahneman named the planning fallacy, and that a buffer lets you stay calm and keep the essential on track when things go wrong. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Joseph, in the Old Testament, read Pharaoh's dream of seven fat cows and seven thin ones as seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine. Egypt stored food during the good years and had food when the famine came.

chapters.title: Subtract: Bring Forth More by Removing Obstacles
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to get more done by removing the obstacles that hold back the essential, instead of adding more effort. His steps are to be clear on your essential intent, to identify the slowest hiker, meaning the single biggest constraint holding everything back, and then to remove that obstacle. His reason is that a whole system moves only as fast as its slowest part, so fixing anything else adds little. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: In Eliyahu Goldratt's novel The Goal, the factory manager Alex leads a scout troop on a hike that keeps stretching out behind the slowest boy, Herbie. Alex puts Herbie at the front and shares out the weight in his pack among the other boys, and the whole troop moves faster.

chapters.title: Progress: The Power of Small Wins
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to make progress through small, steady wins rather than big dramatic pushes. His tools are to focus on minimum viable progress, meaning the smallest useful step forward, to start early and small, and to reward visible progress. His reason is that a sense of progress motivates people and builds momentum toward the essential. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Ward Clapham, a police superintendent in Richmond, Canada, had his officers give young people positive tickets for doing something good, and repeat offending among young people fell.

chapters.title: Flow: The Genius of Routine
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to build routines that make doing the essential automatic, so you do not have to spend willpower deciding each time. He draws on the habit loop of cue, routine and reward, and advises tying the right routine to a clear cue and tackling the hardest thing first. His reason is that a good routine lets the essential happen by default, freeing your mind for other things. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Michael Phelps followed a fixed pre-race routine built with his coach Bob Bowman, and he won.

chapters.title: Focus: What's Important Now?
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to focus on what is important right now, rather than being pulled by the past or the future. His tool is the question What is important now. His reason is that you can only do the essential well when your attention is fully on the task in front of you. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Larry Gelwix, coach of the Highland High School rugby team, taught his players to keep asking what was important now during play (the letters spell WIN), which kept them on the play in front of them, and his team won almost every game and many national championships.

chapters.title: Be: The Essentialist Life
chapters.keys: McKeown tells you to make Essentialism a way of being, not a technique you pull out now and then. He says the Essentialist chooses, discerns and trades off as a constant habit, and that the practice gets easier and becomes part of who you are over time. His reason is that living this way lets you put your full self into the few things that matter most and live with purpose rather than being pulled by everyone else. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Mahatma Gandhi, he says, stripped away nearly everything nonessential from his life: he made his own cloth, stayed away from newspapers and owned fewer than ten things when he died.
